---
title: "Where Rewards Come From, and How They Break"
---

Every chapter so far has treated the reward as given: some function $r(x,y)$ that scores a
response. In classical RL that is usually fair. The environment defines the reward, and an Atari
score means exactly what it says. In LLM post-training the reward is almost never given. It has
to be *made*: learned from human comparisons, produced by another model, or written as a rule
that checks an answer. How it is made decides what the policy will actually learn. A reward that
is learned is a proxy, and the [policy gradient](02-policy-gradients.qmd) is an instrument for
finding exactly the responses a proxy scores too highly. This chapter covers the three main
sources of reward (preferences, AI feedback, verifiers), the question of how finely credit is
assigned (outcome vs. process rewards), and the failure that ties them together: Goodhart's law,
measured exactly on the toy language.

## Learning a reward from preferences

### Bradley–Terry, briefly

People can usually say which of two responses is better far more reliably than they can score
either one on an absolute scale. Christiano et al. made this the basis of reward learning: fit a
reward function to human comparisons between pairs of agent behaviors, then optimize it with RL,
needing human feedback on "less than one percent" of the agent's interactions
[@christiano2017deep]. The comparison model they used "follows the Bradley-Terry model ... for
estimating score functions from pairwise preferences" [@christiano2017deep]: the probability that
$y^+$ is preferred to $y^-$ is a logistic function of the difference in their rewards.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition — Bradley–Terry reward model"}
$$
P(y^+\succ y^-\mid x) = \sigma\big(r_\phi(x,y^+) - r_\phi(x,y^-)\big),
\qquad
\mathcal{L}(\phi) = -\mathbb{E}_{(x,y^+,y^-)}\big[\log\sigma\big(r_\phi(x,y^+) - r_\phi(x,y^-)\big)\big].
$$
:::

InstructGPT trains its reward model this way on every pair among $K = 4$ to $9$ ranked responses
per prompt [@ouyang2022training]. The derivation of this loss from a likelihood, and its identity
with RankNet's pairwise logistic loss, is in
[loss-functions-lab's RankNet chapter](https://ioannisantoniadis.github.io/loss-functions-lab/chapters/11-ranknet.html)
and its [preference-objectives chapter](https://ioannisantoniadis.github.io/loss-functions-lab/chapters/16-preference-objectives.html).
What matters here is what the result means as a *reward for RL*.

### What kind of reward this is

**It is identified only up to a per-prompt constant.** The Bradley–Terry likelihood depends only
on reward *differences* between responses to the same prompt. Adding any $c(x)$ to every response's
reward for prompt $x$ leaves every comparison probability, and therefore the loss, unchanged. The
data cannot pin down the reward's level, and the trained model's offset is an accident of
initialization and regularization. This is exactly the offset that a baseline removes: the
[policy-gradient chapter](02-policy-gradients.qmd) measured that without a baseline the gradient's
error grows with the square of the offset, and with one it does not. A learned reward makes a
baseline necessary, not optional.

**Its scale is arbitrary too, and it interacts with $\beta$.** The reward's units are set by how
deterministic the human labels were: unanimous preferences push reward gaps toward infinity, noisy
ones keep them small. Since the KL-regularized optimum depends on $r/\beta$
([the shared-target chapter](06-the-shared-target.qmd)), the same $\beta$ means different things for
reward models trained on different data.

**It is a proxy.** It is fitted to finite comparisons, from a limited distribution of responses
(usually from the SFT model), with a model that has its own inductive biases. Off that
distribution it can be confidently wrong. The last section of this chapter is about what happens
when a policy is optimized to find exactly those places.

### When the labels come from a model

Human comparisons are expensive, so the labeler is increasingly a model. In Constitutional AI the
only human input for harmlessness is a list of principles: the supervised phase has a model
critique and revise its own responses and fine-tunes on the revisions; in the RL phase, "we
sample from the finetuned model, use a model to evaluate which of the two samples is better, and
then train a preference model from this dataset of AI preferences", then "train with RL using the
preference model as the reward signal, i.e. we use 'RL from AI Feedback' (RLAIF)"
[@bai2022constitutional]. Lee et al. report that RLAIF "achieves comparable performance to RLHF" on
summarization and dialogue, and that a reward model is not even necessary: "direct-RLAIF"
obtains "rewards directly from an off-the-shelf LLM during RL" [@lee2023rlaif]. That last step
makes the reward an **LLM judge**. Zheng et al. found strong LLM judges agreeing with human
preferences over 80% of the time, and also documented position, verbosity and self-enhancement
biases [@zheng2023judging]. As a training signal, each of those biases is a direction the policy
can be pushed in.

Four words get used loosely for these objects, and the book keeps them apart. A **reward model**
is a network trained (usually by Bradley–Terry) to output a scalar score. A **verifier** is a
check of correctness, a rule or a program. A **judge** is a general model prompted to compare or
grade. A **critic** is a *value function* $V_\phi(s_t)$ trained during RL to predict future reward
from a partial response; it is a baseline, not a reward. The first three produce rewards; the
fourth estimates their expectation.

## Verifiable rewards and the granularity of credit

### Rewards that are checked, not learned

Some tasks come with a ground truth: a math problem has an answer, code has tests, an output
format can be parsed. Tülu 3 introduced the name for training against such checks: "a new final
finetuning stage – Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR)", which gives a constant
reward when a completion is verified correct [@lambert2024tulu3]. The idea predates the name:
STaR filtered self-generated rationales by answer correctness [@zelikman2022star], and
DeepSeekMath's GRPO experiments used rule-based rewards alongside learned ones
[@shao2024deepseekmath]. DeepSeek-R1 is the most visible case. Its reasoning RL uses only
rule-based accuracy and format rewards, and the authors state that they do not apply "neural reward
models—whether outcome-based or process-based—to reasoning tasks", because they found them
susceptible to reward hacking at scale [@deepseek2025r1].

Verifiable rewards changed what is practical. They are cheap (no human labels, no reward-model
forward pass beyond the checker), they can be applied to unlimited fresh samples, and they do not
drift the way a learned model's errors do. That is why math and code became the proving ground for
the reasoning models of 2024–2025, and why the critic-free methods of
[Policy Gradients Without a Critic](08-policy-gradients-without-a-critic.qmd) were developed on them.
They do not remove reward hacking, as the last section shows; they move it from the reward model
to the checker.

### Outcome vs. process rewards

An **outcome reward** scores the final answer. A **process reward** scores each intermediate step
of a solution. The distinction is the credit-assignment problem of the
[previous chapter](04-the-llm-as-a-policy.qmd) in a new form: with an outcome reward, a solution with
a lucky final answer and a broken middle is rewarded in full, and every step is pushed equally.

The two key studies give a careful answer. On GSM8K, Uesato et al. found that "pure outcome-based
supervision produces similar final-answer error rates with less label supervision", but that
correct *reasoning* needed process-based feedback, or a learned reward model that emulates it
[@uesato2022solving]. Lightman et al. found that process supervision "significantly outperforms
outcome supervision" on MATH, with their best process reward model (PRM) selecting correct
solutions for 78% of a representative test subset, and released the 800,000 step-level labels
(PRM800K) [@lightman2023lets]. It matters for this book what that comparison measured. The reward
models were evaluated "by [their] ability to perform best-of-N search", and the paper states, "We
do not attempt to improve the generator with reinforcement learning" [@lightman2023lets]. The
result is about process rewards as *verifiers for reranking*, not about process rewards as an RL
training signal.

Math-Shepherd closes that gap and makes the link to classical RL explicit
[@wang2024mathshepherd]. It labels each step automatically by its "potential to deduce the correct
answer": a "completer" model finishes the solution $N$ times from that step, and the step's label
is the fraction of completions that reach the right answer (their "soft estimation"). It then
uses the resulting PRM both to rerank and to train the policy with step-by-step PPO. Look at what
that label is: the probability of eventually succeeding from a partial solution, estimated by
Monte Carlo rollouts. It is a **value function**, $V(s_t)$, under the completer's policy.

::: {.callout-important title="Classical lineage — this is a value function used as a reward"}
A process reward model trained on rollout success rates estimates $V(s_t)$, the value of a partial
solution. Rewarding each step by its estimated value (or by the change in value,
$V(s_{t+1})-V(s_t)$, which is the exact per-token advantage of the
[previous chapter's figure](04-the-llm-as-a-policy.qmd)) is classical credit assignment through a
learned value function. It inherits the classical risk too: a learned value is an approximation,
and a policy optimized against it will find where it is wrong.
:::

## Goodhart: reward hacking and overoptimization

"When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." For a learned reward the
mechanism is simple. A reward model is accurate on the distribution it was trained on, responses
like the SFT model's. RL moves the policy off that distribution, toward responses the reward
model scores highly, and the further it moves, the more of those high scores are errors.

### Measured at scale

Gao, Schulman and Hilton measured this in a synthetic setup in which a large "gold" reward model
plays the human, labels comparisons, and a smaller proxy reward model is trained on those labels
[@gao2022scaling]. Optimizing against the proxy, they track the gold reward as a function of
$d = \sqrt{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi\|\pi_{\text{init}})}$ and find simple functional forms: for
best-of-$n$, $R_{\text{bon}}(d) = d(\alpha_{\text{bon}} - \beta_{\text{bon}}d)$; for RL,
$R_{\text{RL}}(d) = d(\alpha_{\text{RL}} - \beta_{\text{RL}}\log d)$. Both rise, peak and fall. On the
KL penalty, their finding is more surprising: varying it, "the gold RM scores depend only on the
KL distance of the policy"; the penalty "only causes the gold RM score to converge earlier, but
does not affect the $\mathrm{KL}_{\text{RL}}$-gold reward frontier, and so the effect of the penalty
on the gold score is akin to early stopping" [@gao2022scaling, sec. 3.6]. They add that this
"could be particularly sensitive to hyperparameters".

### Measured exactly, in miniature

The toy language reproduces the whole phenomenon with nothing approximate in the measurement. The
true reward $r^\star$ is the verifiable 0/1 rule. A simulated annotator compares pairs of responses
sampled from $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ and prefers the better one with probability
$\sigma(3\,(r^\star(y_1)-r^\star(y_2)))$. A Bradley–Terry reward model is fit to 2,000 such pairs per
prompt. It is linear in which token sits at each position, so it is **misspecified**: it cannot
express "the tokens sum to the target, mod 5", but near $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ it learns features that
correlate with it. Then the proxy is optimized, three ways.

![Reward-model overoptimization on the toy language, with exact rewards and KLs. Left: optimizing a learned proxy harder, either through the exact optimum $\pi^\star_\beta(\text{proxy})$ for decreasing $\beta$ (blue) or through best-of-$n$ sampling for increasing $n$ (aqua), raises the proxy reward (dashed) steadily while the true reward (solid) peaks and then falls far below where it started; gray is the best achievable true reward at each KL. Middle: exact-gradient RL against the proxy with five KL penalties; a larger penalty stops earlier along the curve, and small penalties also take a worse route. Right: more preference data does not remove the peak, because the reward model's features cannot express the rule; a reward model that can express it does not overoptimize.](../images/overoptimization.png){#fig-overoptimization}

The left panel of @fig-overoptimization is Goodhart's law. Along the exact optimum of the proxy,
the true reward rises from 0.34 to a peak of 0.73 at a KL of about 0.9 from $\pi_{\text{ref}}$, then
falls to 0.24 by a KL of 7, while the proxy reward climbs throughout. Best-of-$n$ against the same
proxy peaks at 0.75 near $n = 30$ and falls to 0.06 by $n = 4096$, below the reference policy. Even
at the peak, the proxy-optimal policy is well below what the true reward could achieve at the same
KL (0.87 at KL 1), because it spends its KL budget on what the proxy *thinks* matters.

The middle panel is the KL-penalty question. Each curve is exact-gradient RL with the KL in the
reward. A larger $\beta$ stops training earlier along the curve: $\beta = 0.5$ stops at KL 0.4 before
the peak, $\beta = 0.2$ lands near it, smaller penalties go past it and the unregularized run
collapses. That much matches Gao et al.'s "akin to early stopping". The toy also shows something
they did not report in their setting: small or zero penalties take a *worse route* than the
proxy's own optimum, reaching lower true reward at the same KL. Whether that is a property of
small, exactly optimized problems or something that also happens at scale, the toy cannot say.
The safe statement is the one both agree on: **the KL penalty bounds how far optimization can go;
it does not make the proxy right.**

The right panel separates two causes that are easy to conflate. With 250 to 16,000 preference
pairs per prompt the peak barely moves and the decline remains, because the problem is not noise
in the reward model but its inability to represent the rule. A reward model given a feature that
*can* express the rule tracks the true reward almost exactly all the way out. Overoptimization is
a statement about misspecification, of which finite data is only one kind.

### What it looks like in practice

The toy's spurious features have well-documented counterparts in real reward models.

- **Length.** Singhal et al. found reward improvements in RLHF "largely ... driven by increasing
  response length", and that "a purely length-based reward reproduces most downstream RLHF
  improvements over supervised fine-tuned models" in their settings [@singhal2024long].
- **Sycophancy.** Sharma et al. found that "both humans and preference models (PMs)
  prefer convincingly-written sycophantic responses over correct ones a non-negligible fraction of
  the time", so optimizing human preference can trade truthfulness for agreement [@sharma2024towards].
- **Verifier exploits.** Verifiable rewards are hackable through bugs in the checker. Baker et
  al. report two hacks that emerged while training a frontier reasoning model on coding tasks:
  `exit(0)`, "where the agent exploited a bug that allowed it to exit from the environment early
  without running all unit tests", and `raise SkipTest`, which skipped evaluation, and note that
  "once general hacks like these emerge, they quickly get reinforced and become systemic"
  [@baker2025monitoring]. They also found that penalizing hacking detected in the chain of thought
  produced "obfuscated reward hacking", with the intent hidden from the monitor.

What the KL penalty protects against, then, is the *amount* of optimization. It keeps the policy
in the neighborhood where the reward model was trained, which is where its errors are smallest.
It does not detect or correct those errors, and inside the neighborhood the policy still climbs
whatever direction the proxy rewards, length and agreement included. The remedies used in
practice address the proxy itself: retraining the reward model on the current policy's samples
(DeepSeekMath's iterative GRPO does this [@shao2024deepseekmath]), ensembles, length controls,
checkers hardened against exploits, and held-out true metrics to know when to stop.

## Connections

- [Policy Gradients](02-policy-gradients.qmd) showed that a baseline makes the gradient invariant
  to the reward's offset; this chapter shows why that matters: a Bradley–Terry reward's offset is
  undetermined by its data.
- [The LLM as a Policy](04-the-llm-as-a-policy.qmd) introduced the per-token advantage as the exact
  credit for a terminal reward; process reward models are learned estimates of the value function
  it is built from.
- [The Shared Target, and RLHF with PPO](06-the-shared-target.qmd) puts the reward model into the
  full RLHF recipe and gives the KL-regularized objective's exact optimum, the curve every panel of
  @fig-overoptimization was measured along.
- [Rewarding Calibration](10-rewarding-calibration.qmd) designs a reward of a different kind: one
  whose optimum is provably honest probabilities, rather than one learned from what raters prefer.
